title: General properties of waves
summary: A [[wave|wave]] carries [[energy|energy]] from place to place, but the material it travels through stays where it is. Learn the two kinds of wave, the words that describe them, the wave equation $v = f\lambda$, and how a [[ripple-tank|ripple tank]] shows [[reflection|reflection]], [[refraction|refraction]] and [[diffraction|diffraction]].

goals.text: Explain that a wave transfers energy but not matter, using waves on ropes, springs and water.
Tell [[transverse-wave|transverse]] and [[longitudinal-wave|longitudinal]] waves apart, and give examples of each.
Describe a wave using [[wavefront|wavefront]], [[wavelength|wavelength]], [[frequency|frequency]], crest, trough, [[amplitude|amplitude]] and [[wave-speed|wave speed]].
Use the wave equation $v = f\lambda$ to find a [[speed|speed]], frequency or wavelength.
Describe reflection, refraction and diffraction, and how a [[ripple-tank|ripple tank]] shows each one.
Describe how the wavelength and the size of a gap change how much waves diffract through a gap or round an edge.

before.prompt: A cyclist travels $150\ \text{m}$ in $25\ \text{s}$ at a steady speed. What is her speed, in m/s?
before.hint: Speed is distance travelled divided by the time taken.

before.prompt: A pendulum makes $20$ complete oscillations in $32\ \text{s}$. What is the time for one oscillation, in s?
before.hint: Divide the total time by the number of oscillations.

blocks.text: Drop a stone into a still pond. Ripples spread out, and a leaf floating nearby bobs up and down as they pass. The leaf is not carried outwards with the ripples.

A [[wave|wave]] transfers [[energy|energy]] from one place to another without transferring matter. Each bit of water only vibrates about its own rest position and passes the disturbance on to the next bit.
A rope or a long spring behaves the same way. Shake one end and a wave travels along it, but the rope and coils stay put.

blocks.alt: Two waves travelling to the right. Top: a rope shaken up and down at its left end makes a wave of crests and troughs. A double-headed arrow shows the vibration is up and down, at right angles to the arrow showing the direction of travel. Bottom: a spring pushed and pulled along its length at its left end. The coils are close together in some places and spread apart in others. A double-headed arrow shows the vibration is left and right, parallel to the direction of travel.
blocks.caption: Rope: vibration across the direction of travel. Spring: vibration along it.

blocks.text: In a [[transverse-wave|transverse wave]], each bit of the rope moves across the line the wave moves along, at $90^\circ$ to it. In a [[longitudinal-wave|longitudinal wave]], each coil moves back and forth along the same line the wave moves along. The coils bunch together in some places and spread apart in others.

Modelled as transverse: light and all other electromagnetic radiation, waves on water, and S-waves (secondary seismic waves). Modelled as longitudinal: sound and P-waves (primary seismic waves). A memory hook: S for sideways, P for push–pull.

blocks.question: A small plastic ball floats in the middle of a swimming pool. A swimmer at one end makes waves that pass the ball. Describe how the ball moves, and explain what the waves transfer across the pool.
steps: Say what the ball does, say what happens to the water, then name what is transferred.
blocks.answer: The ball moves up and down as each wave passes. It stays in about the same place and is not carried along with the waves. The water only vibrates about its rest position, so no water is transferred across the pool. The waves transfer energy across the pool.

verify.truth: ball moves up and down; not carried along; water vibrates about its rest position; energy is transferred, not water
requires: stays in about the same place
forbids: carried along with the waves to

blocks.text: Thinking sound carries air from a loudspeaker to your ear. The air only vibrates backwards and forwards; it is the energy that travels.

blocks.prompt: Sound travels from a drum to a listener across a hall. What does the sound wave transfer from the drum to the listener?
blocks.hint: Does the air near the drum end up at the listener?
blocks.explain: The air particles vibrate about their own positions and stay in the hall. Only energy travels from the drum to the listener.

blocks.prompt: Which of these waves can be modelled as longitudinal?
blocks.explain: P-waves and sound are longitudinal. S-waves, light (like all electromagnetic radiation) and water waves are transverse.

blocks.alt: Left: a graph of displacement against distance for a wave at one instant, drawn about a horizontal line labelled rest position. The highest points are labelled crest (peak) and the lowest points trough. A double-headed arrow from one crest to the next crest is labelled wavelength. A vertical double-headed arrow from the rest position up to a crest is labelled amplitude. Right: the same kind of wave seen from above, drawn as five parallel straight lines labelled wavefronts, with an arrow at right angles to them showing the direction of travel. The gap between two neighbouring wavefronts is labelled wavelength.
blocks.caption: Amplitude is measured from the rest position, not from a trough.

blocks.text: A crest (or peak) is a highest point of the wave, and a trough is a lowest point. The [[amplitude|amplitude]] is the greatest distance a point moves from its rest position: from the rest position to a crest.
The [[wavelength|wavelength]] $\lambda$ (the Greek letter lambda) is the distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, such as crest to crest.

Seen from above, water waves look like a set of lines. Each line is a [[wavefront|wavefront]], joining points on the same crest. Wavefronts are at $90^\circ$ to the way the wave is moving, and neighbouring wavefronts are one wavelength apart.
The [[frequency|frequency]] $f$ is the number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz). The [[wave-speed|wave speed]] $v$ is the distance a crest travels each second, in m/s.

blocks.alt: Graph of displacement in cm, from minus 3.0 to plus 3.0, against distance in cm, from 0 to 120, with grid lines every 5 cm across and every 0.5 cm up. The wave starts at zero displacement at 0 cm and rises to a crest of plus 2.5 cm at 15 cm. It falls through zero at 30 cm to a trough of minus 2.5 cm at 45 cm, back to zero at 60 cm, a second crest of plus 2.5 cm at 75 cm, zero at 90 cm, a second trough of minus 2.5 cm at 105 cm and zero again at 120 cm.
blocks.caption: A wave on a long rope at one instant.

blocks.question: The graph shows a wave on a long rope at one instant. Use it to find the wavelength of the wave.
steps: One wavelength runs from a crest to the next crest.
The crests are at $15\ \text{cm}$ and $75\ \text{cm}$ on the distance axis.
Check: trough to trough, $105 - 45$, also gives $60\ \text{cm}$. The distance from $0$ to the first crest is only a quarter of a wavelength.

blocks.prompt: Read from the same graph: what is the amplitude of the wave, in cm?
blocks.hint: Measure from the rest position (zero displacement) up to a crest.
blocks.explain: The crests reach $+2.5\ \text{cm}$ and the rest position is $0$, so the amplitude is $2.5\ \text{cm}$. Crest to trough, $5.0\ \text{cm}$, is twice the amplitude.

blocks.question: As waves pass a fishing float, it bobs up and down $45$ times in $30\ \text{s}$. Calculate the frequency of the waves.
steps: Each complete bob is one wave passing the float.
Frequency is the number of waves each second: $f = \frac{45}{30} = 1.5$, in Hz.

blocks.prompt: The vertical distance from a crest of a wave to the bottom of the next trough is $8.0\ \text{cm}$. What is the amplitude?
blocks.explain: Crest to trough is twice the amplitude, so the amplitude is $\frac{8.0}{2} = 4.0\ \text{cm}$.

blocks.text: Suppose 4 waves pass you each second and each one is $2\ \text{m}$ long. Then the waves move $4 \times 2 = 8\ \text{m}$ every second. So wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
Here $v$ is the wave speed in m/s, $f$ is the frequency in Hz and $\lambda$ is the wavelength in m. Rearranged, $f = \frac{v}{\lambda}$ and $\lambda = \frac{v}{f}$.

blocks.question: A vibrating bar in a tray of water makes ripples with a frequency of $6.0\ \text{Hz}$ and a wavelength of $3.5\ \text{cm}$. Calculate the speed of the ripples in m/s.
A whistle gives out sound of frequency $1500\ \text{Hz}$. The speed of sound in air is $330\ \text{m/s}$. Calculate the wavelength of the sound.
steps: Check: $1500 \times 0.22 = 330$, the speed you started with.

blocks.text: "Calculate" questions: write the equation, substitute the numbers, then give the answer with its unit. Convert cm to m and kHz or MHz to Hz before you substitute.

blocks.prompt: A radio station broadcasts at $1.5\ \text{MHz}$. Radio waves travel at $3.0 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}$. What is the wavelength, in m?
A student shakes the end of a long rope three times as often as before. The waves still travel along the rope at the same speed. How does their wavelength compare with before?

options.text: it becomes one third as long
it becomes three times as long
it becomes one ninth as long

blocks.explain: With $v$ fixed, $f \times \lambda$ stays the same. If $f$ is three times as large, $\lambda$ must be one third as long.

verify.truth: it becomes one third as long

blocks.text: A [[ripple-tank|ripple tank]] is a shallow tray of water with a clear bottom. It shows three things waves can do: bounce off a surface, change direction as they change speed, and spread out.
A motor vibrates a straight bar touching the water, making straight wavefronts. A lamp above shines through the water onto paper below, so the crests show up as bright lines.

blocks.alt: Four ripple-tank patterns seen from above, with wavefronts drawn as lines. Top left, reflection: straight wavefronts travel down towards a straight barrier set at 45 degrees. After reflection, straight wavefronts travel away to the left, at the same angle to the barrier, with the same spacing. Top right, refraction: straight wavefronts in deep water on the left travel down and to the right at an angle towards a boundary with a shaded region of shallow water on the right. In the shallow water the wavefronts are closer together and the direction of travel has turned to be closer to the line at right angles to the boundary. Bottom left, diffraction through a narrow gap: straight wavefronts arrive at a barrier with a gap about one wavelength wide. Beyond the gap the wavefronts are curved arcs centred on the gap, spreading into the regions behind the barrier, with the same spacing as before. Bottom right, diffraction at an edge: straight wavefronts pass the end of a barrier that blocks only the lower half. Beyond it the upper parts stay straight and the lower parts curve round the edge into the region behind the barrier, with the same spacing.
blocks.caption: What you see from above in a ripple tank. Only refraction changes the spacing.

blocks.text: [[reflection|Reflection]]: put a flat barrier in the water. The waves bounce off it. The reflected wavefronts leave at the same angle to the barrier as the incoming ones, with the same wavelength.

[[refraction|Refraction]]: lay a flat glass or plastic plate on the bottom to make a shallow region. Waves travel more slowly in shallow water, so their wavelength is shorter there. If they reach the boundary at an angle, the change of speed also changes their direction.
The frequency does not change when waves refract: the vibrating bar sets it. Only the speed and wavelength change.

[[diffraction|Diffraction]]: leave a narrow gap between two barriers. Beyond the gap, the waves spread out into the region behind the barriers, with curved wavefronts. With a single barrier, the waves also curve round its edge into the region behind it.
Changing the spacing when you draw diffracted wavefronts. Diffraction does not change the speed or the wavelength, so keep the same spacing as the incoming waves.

blocks.question: Describe how a ripple tank can be used to show the refraction of water waves.
steps: Say what you put in the tank, then what happens to the speed, the spacing and the direction of the wavefronts.
blocks.answer: Place a flat glass plate on the bottom of part of the ripple tank, so the water above it is shallow. Use the vibrating bar to send straight waves towards the edge of the plate at an angle. The waves travel more slowly in the shallow water. Their wavelength becomes shorter, so the wavefronts are closer together over the plate. The waves change direction at the boundary between the deep and shallow water.

verify.truth: glass plate makes shallow region; waves slow down there; wavelength shorter (wavefronts closer together); direction changes at the boundary

blocks.question: The bar of a ripple tank vibrates at $12\ \text{Hz}$. A photograph of the shallow region includes a ruler lying in the water. It shows $6$ neighbouring wavefronts spanning $6.0\ \text{cm}$ from the first to the last. Calculate the speed of the waves in the shallow water.
steps: $6$ wavefronts have $5$ gaps between them, so the $6.0\ \text{cm}$ is $5$ wavelengths.
Give 2 significant figures, as in the data.

blocks.text: Paper 5/6: measure across many wavefronts and divide by the number of gaps, not the number of lines. This gives a more accurate wavelength than measuring one gap.

blocks.prompt: Water waves pass from deep water into shallow water. Which quantity stays the same?
blocks.hint: What sets how many waves arrive each second?
blocks.explain: The source sets the frequency. In shallow water the speed falls, so the wavelength gets shorter.

blocks.prompt: Sound from a radio in a classroom spreads out through the open doorway into the corridor. Which wave effect is this?
blocks.hint: Which effect is waves spreading out after a gap?
blocks.explain: Waves spreading out as they pass through a gap is diffraction. Refraction needs a change of speed; reflection needs a surface to bounce off.

blocks.text: How much waves spread out depends on the size of the gap compared with the wavelength. They diffract most when the gap is about one wavelength wide: the wavefronts beyond it are almost semicircles.
When the gap is much wider than the wavelength, most of each wavefront passes through straight. The waves spread only a little, at the edges.

blocks.alt: Two ripple-tank patterns seen from above, with the same wavelength arriving at a barrier. Left: the gap is about one wavelength wide. Beyond it the wavefronts are almost semicircles centred on the gap, spreading well into the regions behind the barrier. Right: the gap is about five wavelengths wide. Beyond it the wavefronts stay mostly straight across the width of the gap and curve only slightly at their ends, so the waves spread very little. The spacing of the wavefronts is the same before and after both gaps.
blocks.caption: Same wavelength, different gaps.

blocks.text: So when the gap is wider than the wavelength, a narrower gap or a longer wavelength gives more spreading. At an edge, longer wavelengths bend further round into the region behind the barrier; very short wavelengths hardly bend at all.

blocks.question: You can hear people talking in the next room through an open doorway, but you cannot see them round the edge of the doorway. Explain this in terms of diffraction.
steps: Compare each wavelength with the width of the doorway, then say how much each wave spreads.
blocks.answer: Sound and light both diffract at the doorway. Speech has wavelengths from tens of centimetres to a few metres, similar to the width of the doorway. So the sound diffracts a lot and spreads round into the room. Light has a wavelength of less than a millionth of a metre, much smaller than the doorway. So light diffracts very little and carries on in almost straight lines, and you cannot see round the edge.

verify.truth: sound wavelength similar to doorway width so diffracts a lot; light wavelength much smaller so diffracts very little

blocks.prompt: Water waves pass through a gap in a harbour wall that is much wider than their wavelength. Which change makes them spread out more beyond the gap?
blocks.hint: Diffraction is greatest when the gap and the wavelength are about the same size.

options.text: increase the amplitude of the waves
increase the frequency of the waves

blocks.explain: A narrower gap is closer in size to the wavelength, so the waves spread more. A higher frequency at the same speed means a shorter wavelength, which spreads less. Amplitude has no effect.

blocks.prompt: Sea waves of several different wavelengths pass the end of a long breakwater. Which waves bend furthest round into the sheltered water behind it?
blocks.hint: Which wavelengths diffract most at an edge?

options.text: the waves with the longest wavelength
the waves with the shortest wavelength
the waves with the largest amplitude
all the waves bend by the same amount

blocks.explain: At an edge, the longer the wavelength, the more the waves diffract round into the region behind the barrier.

verify.truth: the waves with the longest wavelength

blocks.text: A wave transfers energy from place to place without transferring matter.
Transverse: vibration at $90^\circ$ to the direction the wave moves (electromagnetic radiation, water waves, S-waves). Longitudinal: vibration parallel to it (sound, P-waves).
Amplitude: rest position to crest. Wavelength $\lambda$: crest to the next crest. Frequency $f$: waves passing a point per second, in Hz. Neighbouring wavefronts are one wavelength apart.
Ripple tank: a flat barrier shows reflection; a shallow region shows refraction (slower, shorter wavelength, same frequency); a gap or an edge shows diffraction (same wavelength).

Diffraction through a gap is greatest when the gap is about one wavelength wide. For a gap wider than the wavelength, a narrower gap or a longer wavelength gives more spreading. Longer wavelengths bend further round an edge.

mistakes: Measuring the amplitude from a crest to a trough. That distance is twice the amplitude; measure from the rest position to a crest.
Dividing by the number of wavefronts when measuring across several. $6$ wavefronts span only $5$ wavelengths, so divide by the number of gaps.
Putting a wavelength in cm or a frequency in kHz or MHz straight into $v = f\lambda$. Convert to m and Hz first.
Calling sound transverse because it is a familiar wave. Sound and P-waves are longitudinal.
Saying the frequency changes when waves move into shallow water. The speed and wavelength change; the frequency stays the same.
examTips: "Describe" a ripple tank experiment: say what you put in the tank, then what happens to the spacing and direction of the wavefronts.
When you draw wavefronts after a barrier or gap, use a ruler or compasses. Keep the same spacing as the incoming waves unless the depth changes.
Paper 1/2 multiple-choice questions often label distances on a wave diagram. Check whether each one spans a full wave, part of a wave, or crest to trough before you choose.
